paragraphs: Friend, this one is heavy, and I want to say that once, plainly. Moab is wrecked, and the grief runs from the towns to the fugitives on the road. But look at who is crying along with them: "My heart cries out over Moab" (Isaiah 15:5), and later, "my heart laments for Moab like a harp" (Isaiah 16:11). The LORD's word can bring judgment, and in the same passage the speaker weeps over the ones it falls on.

Now look at what the prophecy names as Moab's trouble. "We have heard of Moab’s pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit, his overflowing arrogance. But his boasting is empty" (Isaiah 16:6). Even when Moab goes to his sanctuary to pray, "it will do him no good" (Isaiah 16:12). I think that's a mirror for us, baker. Pride and busy religious motions can look impressive, and they still can't hold you up when everything shakes.

Then in the middle of the rubble, a door opens. When the oppressor is gone, "in loving devotion a throne will be established in the tent of David," and a judge will sit there "seeking justice and hastening righteousness" (Isaiah 16:5). So the hope isn't in our boasting or our own effort. It's in a faithful King who is full of loving devotion, and that's why my ovens stay ready. Keep your eyes on Him, friend, and remember that the story isn't over.
